title: Fifteen milliliters an hour
objective: Protect kidney function by recognizing nephrotoxic drugs and contrast media and keeping perfusion adequate
secondaryObjectives: Acute kidney injury (AKI) and acute tubular necrosis (ATN), including identifying nephrotoxic agents
Classify acute kidney injury as prerenal, intrarenal or postrenal from its cause, and read creatinine and GFR trends as markers of falling kidney function

sources.cite: StatPearls (StatPearls Publishing, NCBI Bookshelf): Acute Kidney Injury (continuing education activity), last updated not shown on the page
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes of the statpearls.com copy (NCBI refuses automated fetches): KDIGO AKI is a creatinine rise of 'by 0.3 mg/dL or more ... within 48 hours', a rise 'to 1.5 times or more than the baseline of the prior 7 days', or 'Urine volume less than 0.5 mL/kg/h for at least 6 hours'. Prerenal: 'any cause of reduced blood flow to the kidney', with vasoconstriction from 'NSAIDs, iodinated contrast'; ACE inhibitors cause efferent dilation. Intrinsic: ATN from nephrotoxins including 'aminoglycosides, vancomycin'; prolonged prerenal injury can progress to ATN. Postrenal: obstruction, most often bladder outlet. Management: avoid further kidney insults including nephrotoxic drugs, renally adjust medications, monitor urine output; 'The best way to determine if the AKI is prerenal or not is a fluid challenge'; diuretics are for volume overload; renal replacement for 'severe and nonresponsive hyperkalemia, uremic pericarditis, and pulmonary edema'.
Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

brief.situation: 14:00 in a medical ICU. You are Mr. Okafor's nurse. He is 71, 70 kg, on day 3 of pneumonia with sepsis, off vasopressors since yesterday. His hourly urine output has fallen: 30, then 20, then 15 mL.
handover: Antibiotics: the ordered vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. A CT chest with IV contrast was done yesterday afternoon.
PRN orders: the ordered ketorolac for pleuritic pain (he is asking for it), and a night order for the ordered furosemide 'for urine output under 30 mL/h'. His home lisinopril was restarted yesterday.
Unit policy: for urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h, check the catheter first, then call the intensivist; pharmacy reviews renally cleared drugs on request.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Kidney injury progresses while he stays dry and the nephrotoxins continue. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It barely progresses once perfusion is restored and the nephrotoxins are held. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Another NSAID dose: afferent vasoconstriction in a dry kidney. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
A diuretic in a volume-depleted patient: less perfusion, more injury. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of oliguric failure with hyperkalemia needing emergency dialysis. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The intensivist called within 5 minutes of the creatinine result (unit practice).
The intensivist reviews and orders fluid: about 4 min.
The bolus runs and the next hourly output is measured: about 30 min.

then.log: Tubing free, no kinks or clots; the catheter flushes easily; bladder scan 40 mL. No outlet obstruction.
Creatinine 0.9 on admission, 1.1 yesterday, 1.9 today: more than double his baseline. Potassium 5.4. BUN 41.
MAP {map}, heart rate {hr}; dry mucosa, cool hands; lungs clear; net 1.4 L negative over 24 hours with fever.
Vancomycin trough this morning above the target range; IV contrast yesterday; ketorolac given twice overnight; lisinopril restarted yesterday.

why.question: What kind of kidney injury is this, what is causing it, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: AKI by KDIGO (creatinine at least 1.5 times baseline; under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours or more is the output criterion); obstruction ruled out by the catheter check and scan; prerenal from low perfusion plus nephrotoxins (contrast, vancomycin, NSAID, ACE inhibitor), at risk of ATN.
parts.modelAnswer: This is AKI: his creatinine has doubled and his output is under 0.5 mL/kg an hour. The catheter is patent and his bladder is empty, so it isn't postrenal. He's dry with a low MAP, and he's had contrast, vancomycin above target, ketorolac and lisinopril. That's prerenal injury on top of nephrotoxins, heading for ATN.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Holds the NSAID and ACE inhibitor; asks pharmacy to dose the vancomycin; calls the intensivist now for fluid to restore perfusion; does not give a diuretic to a dry patient; watches potassium and lungs.
parts.modelAnswer: Hold the ketorolac and lisinopril, get pharmacy on the vancomycin, and call the intensivist now for a fluid bolus. No furosemide: he's dry and it would cut perfusion further. Then watch his potassium, lungs and hourly output.

noProgress.rationale: AKI with falling output left without a plan for an hour is harm here.

expertPath.text: Check the catheter and scan the bladder: patent, 40 mL. Not obstruction.
Creatinine 0.9 to 1.9; potassium 5.4. Dry, MAP in the low 60s.
Hold the ketorolac and lisinopril; pharmacy on the vancomycin. Call the intensivist.
Start the ordered bolus; no furosemide; document and watch potassium and lungs.

dialysis.headline: Emergency dialysis
dialysis.body: Falling output with a doubled creatinine is AKI. Rule out obstruction, then restore perfusion and stop the nephrotoxins. A diuretic or another NSAID dose in a dry patient makes it worse.

protected.headline: Kidneys protected
protected.body: You ruled out obstruction, recognized prerenal and nephrotoxic AKI, held the NSAID and ACE inhibitor, got pharmacy on the vancomycin and fluid in. That is the expert path.

protectedGaps.headline: Improving, with gaps
protectedGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether the nephrotoxins were held, and whether a diuretic or NSAID went in.

time_up.headline: No plan
time_up.body: AKI needs the cause found and perfusion restored within minutes, not on rounds.

scoring.modelReasoning: His creatinine has more than doubled and his output is under 0.5 mL/kg an hour: AKI. A patent catheter and an empty bladder rule out a postrenal cause. He is dry with a low MAP after fever losses (prerenal), and he has had contrast, vancomycin above target, an NSAID and an ACE inhibitor, all of which injure or underperfuse the kidney and push it toward ATN. Hold the NSAID and ACE inhibitor, have pharmacy dose the vancomycin to his kidney function, call the intensivist for fluid to restore perfusion, and do not give a diuretic to a volume-depleted patient. Watch potassium, lungs and hourly output.

toxQ.ask: While the bolus runs: which of his drugs can cause acute tubular necrosis directly?

choices.label: None; drugs cause only prerenal injury

toxQ.explain: Nephrotoxins such as aminoglycosides and vancomycin cause ATN; NSAIDs and contrast constrict the afferent arteriole and ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent.

kdigoQ.ask: While you assess: which finding alone meets the definition of AKI?

choices.label: A creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours
One hour of urine under 30 mL

kdigoQ.explain: AKI is a creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine under 0.5 mL/kg/h for at least 6 hours.
